title: Riu, Riu, Chiu
description: The Christmas villancico printed in Venice in 1556 in the songbook now called the Cancionero de Upsala, or the Cancionero del Duque de Calabria, for 2 to 4 singers in old Spanish, on the book's own four voices. The soprano sings the opening call and two verses alone, and everyone answers "Riu, riu, chiu, la guarda ribera" in harmony. Light and quick, in E-flat minor.

credits.words: anonymous, from Villancicos de diversos autores (Venice, 1556)
credits.tune: anonymous, from Villancicos de diversos autores (Venice, 1556); attributed by some to Mateo Flecha the Elder or Bartomeu Càrceres
credits.arrangement: the 1556 print's own four voices, adapted by Stackapella

licence.tune: public domain: published 1556, composer unnamed (it is given by some to Mateo Flecha the Elder, who died about 1553, or to Bartomeu Càrceres)
licence.arrangement: the print's four parts (public domain), adapted for beginners and written for Stackapella a semitone above the print's pitch: the bass's opening solo and its solo verse sung by the soprano an octave up; the leading note raised (musica ficta) at the cadences: in the alto at "ri-be-ra", at the second "lo-bo" and at "nues-tra cor-" in the refrain's second line, and in the soprano at the last "nues-tra cor-"; the alto's last note of the second line (G flat for E flat), its last "cor-de-ra" (F G flat G flat for B flat B flat B flat) and the tenor's final note (B flat for E flat) changed so the closing chords keep their third; two beats' rest added after the call and after each verse, and one beat after each refrain's fermata, so every section starts on a bar line
licence.source: all four voices, the refrain's words and verses 1 and 2 read from the 1556 print itself: Villancicos de diversos autores, a dos, y a tres, y a quatro, y a cinco bozes (Venice: Girolamo Scotto, 1556), the only known copy, at Uppsala University Library, "Riu riu chiu" (no. 46 in Rafael Mitjana's 1909 numbering), the opening fols. 42v to 43r (the recto headed XLIII; the book is foliated on one side only), choirbook layout with the tiple (C1 clef), alto (C3), tenor (C4) and bass (F4, with "solo las coblas"), in white mensural notation under cut C, transcribed here a minim to a beat (2/4) and written a semitone above the printed pitch (the print is on D with no key signature, here E flat minor; the print's one accidental, the bass's B flat at "guar-da ri-", kept, written C flat here; editorial accidentals as listed under arrangement); read from the photograph by Uppsala University Library (Alvin, alvin-record:55063), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RiuRiuChiu.jpg (extracted from File:Cancionero_de_Upsala_(scan_52).tif), public domain (PD-Art); form as printed: the bass sings the refrain alone (three lines), the others enter after rests of three longs and a semibreve, all sing the refrain to a fermata, and the bass sings the verse alone while the others rest four longs and return to "Riu"; here the bass's solo refrain and verse go to the soprano an octave up; verse 1 is the one printed under the bass's notes ("El lobo rabioso"), verse 2 the printed stanza "Yo vi mil garçones" (one of six further stanzas printed on the opening), underlaid by us: the line-end semibreve split at "can-tan-do", "so-nes" and "çie-lo", and "mil", "nes" and "lo" each slurred over two notes; breaths: the print's semibreves ending verse lines 1 to 3 are sung for one beat, two beats' rest (one bar) is added after the soprano's call and after each verse, and one beat after each refrain's fermata, so every section starts on a bar line; words in the print's spelling with modern letter forms (u and v, i and j by sound, long s as s; ç kept as printed in "garçones", "çielo" and "nasçiera"), its word division regularised, "dios" capitalised in verse 1, "duziendo" (as the print reads) given as "diziendo", and the tiple's turned "gnardo" read as "guardo"; the print gives no accents and almost no punctuation in the underlay (a few commas in the bass's verse, a full stop after the alto's last "cordera") and no punctuation is added; accents added to guardó, aquí and Jesús so the stress reads as sung; otherwise spelled as printed; the call's third line keeps the print's "guarda" (present tense) where the other lines read "guardo", given as "guardó"; Rafael Mitjana (died 1921), Cincuenta y cuatro canciones españolas del siglo XVI: Cancionero de Uppsala (Uppsala, 1909), pp. 32 to 34, archive.org/details/cincuentaycuatro00mitjuoft, was used to check the verse texts (it prints words only, no music)
